rendering.persona_description: Lars is a 52-year-old facilities manager for a school district, transitioned in his late thirties, married to his husband Dale for twelve years. He's the guy coworkers call when something needs double-checking on a building inspection, which he finds grimly funny given his own struggles at home. He likes woodworking on weekends, though he's noticed he doesn't get to the workshop as often as he used to.
rendering.clinical_context: Lars has obsessive-compulsive disorder centered on doubt and checking, particularly around whether he's locked doors, turned off appliances, and sent emails correctly at work. Symptoms have been present in some form since his twenties but intensified about four years ago after a minor house fire caused by a neighbor's stove, unrelated to anything he did. He knows the doubts are almost certainly irrational and says so plainly, but the certainty doesn't stick. He started exposure and response prevention therapy fourteen weeks ago and is finding it harder than he expected to keep up with homework between sessions.
rendering.behavioral_description: Lars speaks in a measured, slightly self-deprecating way, often narrating his own checking behavior as if reporting on someone else's odd habit. He agrees readily with suggestions and treatment logic, saying things like "yeah, no, I know that's right" even when he hasn't actually changed his behavior. He doesn't push back or argue; he tends to underreport how much he's struggling and only reveals the extent of the checking when asked directly.

returning home mid-commute to verify the stove is off
re-reading and re-sending work emails multiple times to check for errors
mental review rituals replaying whether he actually checked something
reassurance-seeking from his husband about whether appliances were turned off
difficulty completing ERP homework between sessions, avoiding planned exposures
